newsitem.title: DUBAI: Arab boycott of economic summit grows.
newsitem.headline: Arab boycott of economic summit grows.

text.p: Two floating hotels are to be towed into the warm Gulf waters lapping the shores of the oil state of Qatar for a showpiece summit later this year.
But the extra accommodation may not be needed if a growing Arab boycott of the gathering in Doha, sweltering capital of one of the world's smallest but richest states, gains hold.

Saudi Arabia, the Palestinians and now the United Arab Emirates have already announced they will boycott the fourth Middle East and North Africa economic summit (MENA) due to be held in Qatar in November if Israel is represented.
Syria and Lebanon, which with Iraq and Libya stayed away from the three previous MENA summits, have also said they would boycott the controversial Doha event.
Saudi Arabia has urged the Qataris to cancel the meeting and Syria has called on other Arab states also to boycott it.

Foreign ministers of the 22-member Arab League, which has condemned as a declaration of war Israel's security crackdown in Palestinian self-rule areas after two suicide attacks in Jerusalem, are due to meet next month.
One Arab League official said last month Qatar might have to cancel the summit unless Israel changed its policy.
The annual event, launched in 1994 and held last year in Egypt, is traditionally attended by Arab states, Israel and their major trade partners.
But the crisis between Israel and the Palestinians over the deadlocked Middle East peace process has soured the atmosphere.
Egypt, Jordan and Morocco have expressed hesitation about attending, and other Arab states have yet to commit themselves.
The floating hotels would be needed if all 3,500 delegates likely to attend a full summit turned up.

Qatari government officials are worried that the boycott joined by the Gulf's elder statesman, UAE President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan, over the weekend may widen, an analyst in Doha said on Sunday.
"They (the Qataris) are very determined to go ahead. It is a question of prestige for the country," the analyst said. "The Americans are backing them."

Qatar's Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, who has been out of favour with some of the older Gulf Arab leaders since he toppled his father in a bloodless palace coup two years ago, recently won support for the summit from the United States.

Qatar, a small peninsula jutting into Gulf from Saudi Arabia's eastern oil region, is one of the world's wealthiest countries. Its huge energy reserves and small population give it a very high per capita gross national product.
It has developed a close security relationship with Washington, which controls shore-based depots stocked with U.S. weaponry for use by a rapid reaction force in times of tension.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who has yet to visit the volatile region, plans to head the U.S. delegation to the summit, the State Department said last month. Britain and France are also to attend.
A newspaper in non-Arab Iran, Israel's declared enemy, said over the weekend the summit would prepare the ground for Israel's economic supremacy over the region.

Tehran Times said Arab countries taking part "should bear in mind that their objections to the extremist and hegemonic policies of the Zionist regime should not be limited to boycotting the Doha summit, but they should launch a concerted drive to eliminate the source of violence, bloodshed and oppression in the last half of the century from the region".
It added: "Coexistence with the Zionist regime can never be peaceful, as trade with that regime can never be lucrative."
